clue.text: Southern peninsula — get out of here!

parts.note: S = southern
the Hoo Peninsula, a stretch of Kent between the Thames and the Medway

explanation.surface: A traveller in a southern peninsula is told firmly to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: The peninsula is a real place rather than a crossword abbreviation: HOO is a small peninsula in Kent, England.
explanation.definitionFit: SHOO is what you say to send someone or something away, as does 'get out of here!'.

clue.text: Surprise when century is first hundred

parts.note: as = when ('as I left' = 'when I left')
a ton = a hundred, a century
used as it stands

indicators.note: takes the first letter of the word after it

parts.note: first letter of hundred

explanation.surface: Someone is amazed when a batsman's century turns out to be his first hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a century and a hundred are the same thing, which makes the surface sound like a scorecard; here the century is TON and hundred only gives its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, though stronger: to astonish is to surprise so much that it stuns.

clue.text: Pass — despite online error?

parts.note: e- = online, as in e-mail
a lapse = a slip, an error

explanation.surface: Someone gets a pass mark in spite of a mistake made on the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the invented word: an 'e-lapse' would be an error made online.
explanation.definitionFit: Time that elapses passes.

clue.text: Protective layer for fool in grip of Hi-Lo fever

indicators.note: the fool is held inside the other letters
a fever leaves things in a feverish muddle, so the letters of Hi-Lo are jumbled

parts.note: HILO rearranged
a clot = a fool, placed after OIL

explanation.surface: Someone is looking for protection for a fool caught up in a craze for the card game Hi-Lo.
explanation.walkthrough: Hi-Lo looks like a proper name to be left alone, but it is only four letters to rearrange around the fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Oilcloth is cloth treated with oil to make it waterproof, used as a protective covering on tables and shelves.

clue.text: Struggle of five in difficult resit

indicators.note: five goes inside the other letters
the letters of resit are made awkward, rearranged

parts.note: RESIT rearranged
V = five in Roman numerals, placed inside

explanation.surface: Five students battle through a tough exam retake.
explanation.walkthrough: A resit is a British term for a retaken exam; here it only supplies five letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean to make a great effort against difficulty.

clue.text: Pry? That makes sense

definitions.meaning: to pry = to poke into others' business, as a sniffing dog does
the organ of smell, which makes one of the five senses

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether prying is the reasonable explanation, and is told it is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That makes sense' reads as agreement; taken literally, it describes the organ that gives us a sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The nose supplies the sense of smell, and to nose into things is to pry.

clue.text: Two-thirds of Bath is let out in 13/18

indicators.note: let out means the letters of let are released and rearranged
keep four of the six letters of 'Bath is'

parts.note: BATHIS minus its first two letters
LET rearranged

explanation.surface: Part of a house in Bath is let out as a rental in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bath is' reads as the city and a verb; taken together it is a six-letter string to trim. The definition is the song title from 13/18, read as a description.
explanation.definitionFit: The thistle is Scotland's national emblem, its flower, so it is literally the flower of Scotland.

clue.text: Violet Elizabeth's evergreens not available — or they're mostly lost in 13/18

indicators.note: most of the word is lost, leaving only its start

parts.note: firs are evergreens, and Violet Elizabeth's lisp turns FIRS into FIRTH
off = not available, as a dish is off the menu
used as it stands
THEYRE with most of its letters gone

explanation.surface: A lisping child complains that there are no fir trees to be had, or that most of them have vanished in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Violet Elizabeth Bott, from Richmal Crompton's Just William books, lisps 'I'll thcream and thcream'. The pieces run FIRTHOFFORTH, so the double F of 'off' is shared across the space in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Firth of Forth is the estuary of the River Forth, a body of flowing water, so a 'flower' of Scotland.

clue.text: Beggar belief at first, smothered by short cry …

indicators.note: take the first letter of belief
the cry is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: HOOT, a cry, cut short
first letter of belief, placed inside

explanation.surface: A beggar's story is so hard to believe that it is greeted with a stifled cry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beggar belief' is a set phrase meaning 'be hard to believe', which hides that Beggar is the definition. The ellipsis just runs the sentence into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A hobo is a homeless wanderer, a beggar or tramp.

clue.text: … to ban cheat in writing?

indicators.note: the cheat goes inside the writing

parts.note: prose = ordinary writing
to crib = to cheat by copying, placed inside

explanation.surface: Continuing from 9, someone wants to outlaw cheating in written exams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheat in writing' reads as copying in a test; that sense is also why CRIB fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from the Latin for posting someone's name as an outlaw; now it means to forbid.

clue.text: Put your shoe on, professor

parts.note: an oxford is a lace-up shoe
put on = don; 'Put ... on' wraps round the shoe

explanation.surface: An order to a teacher: get your shoes on, professor.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as an order to get dressed; Oxford names both a lace-up shoe and the university, so the shoe brings the professor's university with it.
explanation.definitionFit: Don is the Oxford and Cambridge word for a university teacher, so a professor there is one.

clue.text: The state of an Antrim river

definitions.meaning: a river flowing into Lough Neagh in County Antrim, Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: A question about how healthy a river in Northern Ireland is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The state of' reads as 'the condition of'; instead it is a US state, and Antrim is a county in Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Maine is a US state and also the name of a river in County Antrim.

clue.text: Crazy commanding officer?

parts.note: the commanding officer is the man in charge
I/C = in charge, the abbreviation for the officer in command

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the officer in command has lost his mind.
explanation.walkthrough: I/C is a standard abbreviation for 'in charge'; the question mark admits that the commanding officer is only described, as a MAN I/C.
explanation.definitionFit: Manic means wildly energetic or frenzied, crazy.

clue.text: Town clears off old wrecks for a song

indicators.note: the letters before it are wrecked, broken up and rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 16 letters

explanation.surface: A town sells off its old shipwrecks for next to nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For a song' is a set phrase meaning 'very cheaply', which hides that 'a song' is the definition and 'wrecks' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Flower of Scotland is a song, the unofficial Scottish national anthem sung at rugby and football matches.

clue.text: Low back — acid test of welly?

indicators.note: the word is written backwards

parts.note: to low is to moo, as cattle do; reversed to OOM
pH is the measure of acidity

explanation.surface: A question whether the low back of a Wellington boot is the real test of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Welly' is British for a Wellington rubber boot, but also slang for effort or power, as in 'give it some welly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Oomph means energy or vigour, as does 'welly' in British slang.

clue.text: Monsters, Inc. has part for Edge

parts.note: surface padding: only the film title's last word holds the answer

indicators.note: the answer is part of the words before it

parts.note: the answer runs from 'Inc.' into the first letter of 'has'

explanation.surface: The film Monsters, Inc. has a role going for the actor or musician Edge.
explanation.walkthrough: The italic film title makes 'Monsters, Inc.' look like one unit; only its last word and 'has' hold the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as a verb: both mean to move forward slowly, a little at a time.

clue.text: See 8
Portion made by breaking bread

definitions.meaning: a part or share of something
the name of the moment in the Eucharist when the priest breaks the bread

explanation.surface: A share is produced by tearing a loaf apart.
explanation.walkthrough: In church liturgy the Fraction is the name of the moment when the priest breaks the consecrated bread.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for a part, plus a church term: the rite of breaking the bread in the Eucharist bears the answer as its name.

clue.text: Remove from flight: early sign of pregnancy

definitions.meaning: what an overbooked airline does to a passenger
the swelling of a pregnant belly

explanation.surface: A pregnant woman is taken off her flight because she is showing.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves read as cause and effect, but they are separate meanings of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: An airline's word for taking a booked passenger off an overfull flight, and everyday slang for the swelling of a pregnancy.

clue.text: Athletic feats keeping horses on track

definitions.note: the second definition describes what blinders do, not the things themselves
definitions.meaning: in British slang a blinder is a superb performance: 'he played a blinder'
the eye shades (US name) that stop a racehorse looking sideways

explanation.surface: A racing report on horses running fine races without straying off course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blinder' for an outstanding performance is British slang; 'blinders' for the horse's eye shades is the American name for blinkers.
explanation.definitionFit: Blinders are brilliant performances and also the eye shields that keep a horse looking ahead.

clue.text: See 13
Tired — knackered — embracing unknown number — here?

definitions.note: 'here' stands for a place: the dating app where the tired and lonely meet an unknown number of strangers

indicators.note: the letters of tired are worn out, rearranged

parts.note: TIRED rearranged
n = an unknown number in algebra, placed inside

explanation.surface: An exhausted, worn-out person meets a string of strangers in some place.
explanation.walkthrough: Knackered is British slang for exhausted, so it reads as a synonym of Tired; it is the instruction to rearrange. The definition is loose: Tinder, the dating app, is where you meet unknown numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinder is a dating app, the place the question mark hints at where you meet many strangers.

clue.text: See 24
Mitigate risk of fire

definitions.meaning: a bookmaker lays off a big bet by placing bets elsewhere to spread the risk

explanation.surface: An instruction to reduce the danger of a blaze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Risk of fire' reads as a blaze; fire is really the verb 'dismiss', and 'of' only joins the two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay off a bet reduces a bookmaker's risk, and to lay off staff is to fire them.

clue.text: After scam, South African party's in a mess — it was ever thus

definitions.note: the definition is a clause describing a state that never changes; CONSTANCY is the noun for it

indicators.note: the rest comes after the scam

parts.note: a con = a scam

indicators.note: the party goes inside the mess

parts.note: a sty (pigsty) = a mess
the ANC, African National Congress, placed inside STY

explanation.surface: A political comment: after a fraud, the South African ruling party is in trouble, as it always has been.
explanation.walkthrough: The political surface reads as a sigh about corruption; its closing phrase is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Constancy is the quality of staying the same, just as 'it was ever thus' says nothing has changed.

clue.text: Layer Cake

definitions.meaning: as a verb: to cover thickly, as mud cakes a boot

explanation.surface: Layer Cake, the 2004 crime film, or a layered sponge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Layer Cake' reads as one thing, a film or a sponge, but it is two definitions, and Cake is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for a layer, and as a verb, to cover thickly, which is what mud does when it cakes.

clue.text: Flag cut in return of Irish MP's bill

indicators.note: the word loses its last letter
the MP's letters come back the other way
it goes inside the reversed MP

parts.note: a TD, Teachta Dála, is a member of the Irish parliament; reversed to DT
to flag = to ebb, cut to EB and placed inside

explanation.surface: A weary Irish politician returns home to find an expensive bill waiting.
explanation.walkthrough: Flag is the verb 'tire' (so EBB), not a banner; the Irish MP is a TD, the standard title in the Dáil, Ireland's parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an unpaid bill is money owed.

clue.text: 13/18's bloody start to Ashes?

indicators.note: take the first letter of bloody

parts.note: first letter of bloody
the Ashes, the cricket series, are played for a tiny urn

explanation.surface: Scotland's bloody-minded start to a series of England-Australia cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads the song title literally: a 'flower' is something that flows, so a flower of Scotland is a Scottish stream. A burn is Scottish for a stream.
explanation.definitionFit: A burn is a Scottish stream, water that flows, so a 'flower' of Scotland.

clue.text: 13/18 misrepresented elite — for what?

indicators.note: the letters are presented wrongly, in a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

explanation.surface: The song misrepresents the elite, and someone asks why.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads the song title literally: a 'flower' is something that flows. The Water of Leith is the river running through Edinburgh to the port of Leith.
explanation.definitionFit: The Water of Leith is a river in Scotland, so a flower (flowing thing) of Scotland.

clue.text: Shed tears after empty aquifer found to hold nothing? It's not like that

definitions.note: the definition is a sentence; 'a far cry' is used as a phrase meaning 'very different'

indicators.note: the tears come after the rest
remove the inside of aquifer
the outer letters hold nothing inside

parts.note: AQUIFER with its middle removed
FA = 'sweet FA', British slang for nothing at all; placed inside AR
to cry = to shed tears

explanation.surface: A water engineer weeps on finding an underground reservoir dry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet FA' (sweet Fanny Adams) is British slang for nothing. The phrase 'a far cry from' means very different from, which is what 'It's not like that' says.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that is a far cry from another is very different from it; not like it at all.
